topics.title: Nouns (संज्ञा)
topics.explanation: Sanskrit nouns have three genders (masculine, feminine, neuter), three numbers (singular, dual, plural), and eight cases (vibhakti). The ending of a noun changes based on its gender, number, and case.

examples.note: The visarga (ः) is a common nominative masculine ending.
Many feminine nouns end in -ā in the nominative.
Many neuter nouns end in -am in the nominative.

practice.question: Which gender is the word 'वनम्' (forest)?
practice.explanation: Words ending in -अम् in nominative singular are typically neuter.

topics.title: Pronouns (सर्वनाम)
topics.explanation: Sanskrit has personal pronouns for first person (I/we), second person (you), and third person (he/she/it/they). Third person pronouns also vary by gender.

examples.note: Used regardless of gender.
Used regardless of gender.
Changes by gender: सः (m), सा (f), तत् (n).

practice.question: What is the Sanskrit pronoun for 'she'?
practice.explanation: सा is the feminine third-person singular pronoun.

topics.title: Verbs (क्रिया)
topics.explanation: Sanskrit verbs conjugate based on person (first, second, third) and number (singular, dual, plural). The present tense (लट् लकार) is the most common starting point. Verbs are grouped into classes (gaṇa) based on how the root is modified.

examples.note: Root: गम् (to go). The -ति ending marks third person singular.
The -आमि ending marks first person singular.
The -असि ending marks second person singular.

practice.question: What does गच्छामि mean?
practice.explanation: The -āmi ending is first person singular present tense.

topics.title: Cases (विभक्ति)
topics.explanation: Sanskrit uses eight cases to show the role of a noun in a sentence. The case is shown by changing the ending of the word rather than using prepositions (as English does).

examples.note: First case (प्रथमा विभक्ति) marks the subject.
Second case (द्वितीया विभक्ति) marks the object.
Third case (तृतीया विभक्ति) marks the instrument or accompaniment.

practice.question: In 'रामं पश्यति', what case is रामं?
practice.explanation: रामं is the accusative (object) form. The -अं ending marks the accusative singular for masculine nouns.

topics.title: Gender (लिङ्ग)
topics.explanation: Every Sanskrit noun has a grammatical gender: masculine (पुल्लिङ्ग), feminine (स्त्रीलिङ्ग), or neuter (नपुंसकलिङ्ग). Adjectives must agree in gender with the noun they describe.

examples.note: Masculine nouns often end in -अः in the nominative.
Feminine nouns often end in -आ or -ई in the nominative.
Neuter nouns often end in -अम् in the nominative.

practice.question: What is the gender of 'नदी' (river)?
practice.explanation: नदी ends in -ई, a common feminine ending.

topics.title: Tenses (लकार)
topics.explanation: Sanskrit has ten tense-mood forms called lakāra. The most important for beginners are the present (लट्), past (लङ्), and future (लृट्). Each tense changes the verb endings.

examples.note: Present tense is the starting point for learning conjugation.
Past tense adds अ- prefix (augment) and changes the ending.
Future tense inserts -इष्य- before the ending.

practice.question: What tense is 'गमिष्यति'?
practice.explanation: The -इष्यति ending is a marker of the future tense (लृट् लकार).

topics.title: Sentence Structure (वाक्य रचना)
topics.explanation: The typical Sanskrit sentence follows Subject-Object-Verb (SOV) order. Because case endings already show who does what, word order is flexible, but SOV is the most natural and common.

examples.note: Subject-Object-Verb is the default order.
Same SOV pattern.
Because of case endings, the meaning stays the same even if you rearrange the words.

practice.question: What is the typical word order in Sanskrit?
practice.explanation: Sanskrit typically follows Subject-Object-Verb order, unlike English which uses SVO.
